The lighthouse had not worked in years, but the keeper still climbed the stairs each evening. One hundred and twelve steps, spiraling upward like a question that refused to resolve. He carried no lamp. He lit no flame. He simply stood at the top and looked out at the water, which moved in its ancient, restless way... neither arriving nor departing, merely continuing. His wife had asked him once why he bothered. He said something about duty, but they both knew that was not the whole truth. The whole truth was harder, sharper, shaped like the absence of a son who had gone to sea and never returned. The lighthouse was a vigil. A candle held up to the darkness, even without fire. Every evening, he climbed. Every morning, the sea offered nothing but itself. And still he went. There is a word for this kind of faithfulness, but it lives in a language no one speaks anymore.
